chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Part II done. You can now read every package in the stack. Time for the wire.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Forget "multiplayer" for a second. Look at what is physically there.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Both drivers exist in the same process here. Net Code registers two transports:

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Our host's own client uses I P C; the second Play Mode player uses U D P to loopback. That is why the Play Mode Tools window shows both endpoints on the server row.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: There is no Connection class. A connection is an entity, and its component set is its state machine:

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Read that chain as a checklist. Every "player doesn't spawn" bug is one of those components missing, and the ladder in chapter 19 walks it.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Trap, no ghosts are sent until Network Stream In Game exists on the connection. Not "fewer". None. It is the single flag that arms the whole snapshot system, and it is why chapter 21's client graph matters so much.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: The transport composes pipeline stages per channel:

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a protocol stack assembled from composable shift registers. Each stage owns a slice of per-connection state and hands a buffer to the next.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Snapshots are deliberately unreliable: a lost snapshot is not worth retransmitting, because the next one (20 milliseconds later) already contains newer truth. Commands are the same. Only remote procedure calls and ghost spawn/despawn need reliability.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: That single design decision is why Net Code tolerates packet loss gracefully and why you must never assume a specific tick's data arrived.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Connection Events For Tick is a Native Array<Net Code Connection Event>.Read Only valid for this tick only. Connection State.State walks Unknown then Connecting then Handshake then Approval then Connected then Disconnected.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Nerve's Client Connection Tracker consumes exactly this array and folds it into a durable Client Connection Snapshot in graph state, because the events vanish next tick but the conclusion ("we are disconnected, reason Timeout") must persist.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, the event array is a status register you must read before the next clock edge. The snapshot is the latch you copy it into.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Client Server Bootstrap.Requested Play Type decides which worlds get built:

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: With com.unity.dedicated-server installed, UNITY_USE_MULTIPLAYER_ROLES is defined and Multiplayer Roles override this per virtual player. Chapter 23 shows why that is the difference between a working second player and a port-bind crash.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Probe, what the driver actually bound: ``csharp var d = System API.Get Singleton<Network Stream Driver>(); // Play Mode Tools shows the same thing: [I P C.] [U D P.] ``

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: A ghost is an entity the server owns and mirrors to clients. Our capsule is one. So is the controller.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Ghost Authoring Component on the prefab produces a serialization schema: which components, which fields, at what precision, with what change-detection. Baking generates serializer code per ghost type, no reflection at runtime.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: That third row is the whole design in one dropdown. Chapter 17 unpacks it.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: For a player capsule, Owner Predicted is nearly always right: you need your own capsule to respond in zero frames; you do not need someone else's to be frame-exact, you need it smooth.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Snapshots: delta-compressed, importance-scheduled

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Three consequences you must internalise:

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: A snapshot is not the whole world. It is as much of it as fits in ~1200 bytes, prioritised. Low-importance ghosts update at a lower effective rate. This is a feature. Delta baselines are per connection. The server remembers what each client has ACKed. Loss is normal. The next snapshot re-bases automatically.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, importance scheduling is a weighted round-robin arbiter on a fixed-width bus. You do not get more bandwidth; you get to choose who wastes it.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Fewer bits on the wire, and, crucially, quantized values compare equal more often, so delta compression finds more unchanged fields. Choose per field: position often 1000, rotation 1000, a health value maybe 1.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Trap, quantization is a real precision loss, applied before the client compares predicted vs received. Set it too coarse and prediction will disagree with the server constantly, causing continuous micro-rollbacks that look like jitter. Set it too fine and you burn bandwidth. This is a tuning knob, not a formality.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Ghost Relevancy lets the server decide a ghost simply does not exist for a given connection, interest management, fog of war, zoning. Nerve wraps this in a Relevancy Settings asset, which our project has registered on Server Settings.prefab.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: For two capsules on one map it does nothing. At 200 players it is the difference between shipping and not.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Our capsules are server-spawned: Player Connection System instantiates on the server, and the client materialises them when the snapshot arrives. That is why ghosts=2 appears in the client world without the client ever calling Instantiate.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Probe, see the schema Unity actually generated: `` Multiplayer then Ghost Snapshot Inspector (in play mode) `` It shows per-ghost byte cost. If a ghost is unexpectedly expensive, a field you did not mean to replicate is in the schema.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Chapter 01 said the frame loop is a lousy clock. Net Code builds a good one on top of it. This chapter is that clock.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Simulation Tick Rate is authored in Client Server Tick Rate. Everything on the wire is stamped with a Network Tick, a wrapping uint, so never compare with <. Use tick.Is Newer Than(other), which handles wraparound the way a sequence-number comparison must.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, Network Tick is a wrapping counter with a comparator that understands modular distance. Exactly like TCP sequence numbers. Comparing raw values works for hours and then breaks once, catastrophically.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Three different "nows" on one screen simultaneously. Your capsule is drawn at the predicted tick; the other player's capsule is drawn at the interpolated tick. That is not a bug, that is the entire trade, made explicit.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: A command for tick T must be in the server's hands before the server simulates T. So the client must generate it early, at least one-way latency plus jitter margin. Net Code measures round trip time continuously and adjusts the lead automatically. When the network worsens, the client silently runs further ahead.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Trap, a command that arrives late is dropped, and the server extrapolates from the last input it has. That reads to the player as "my input was eaten". If you see this, look at the command age stats in Play Mode Tools before you look at your input code.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Render at 144 hertz with a 60 hertz simulation and most frames have no new tick. Rendering at the last full tick would visibly stutter. So Net Code runs a partial tick: the prediction group simulates a fraction of a tick purely for presentation, then throws it away and re-runs the full tick when it truly arrives.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Trap, spawn a particle, play a sound, or increment a counter in the prediction group without checking Is First Time Fully Predicting Tick and it happens several times per tick. Every "my gun fires 3 bullets per trigger pull" bug is this.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Continuous integration (moving a transform) is safe in partial ticks. One-shot side effects are not.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: The prediction group runs N times per frame

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: This is why Predicted Simulation System Group is special and why chapter 17 exists.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: System API.Time.Delta Time inside prediction

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Inside the prediction group, the delta is the tick delta, not the frame delta. That is why our movement code is correct without doing anything clever:

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: If it used frame delta, a rollback replaying 10 ticks in one frame would move the capsule 10 frames' worth of distance. Determinism dies, and it dies only under packet loss, which is the worst kind of bug to reproduce.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Higher tick rate = lower input latency, more CPU on the server, more bandwidth, and more rollback work per correction. It multiplies through everything.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Probe, read the live clock: ``csharp var t = System API.Get Singleton<Network Time>(); Debug.Log($"server={t.Server Tick} partial={t.Is Partial Tick} first Full={t.Is First Time Fully Predicting Tick}"); ``

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: The single most important sentence in this book:

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Our component is four bytes and it is the whole protocol:

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: If we sent Position instead, a modified client could write any position it liked and the server would obey. That is client authority, and it is the hole every cheat engine walks through. Unity's own prediction docs open by warning about it.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: What IInput Component Data generates for you

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: You write one struct; the generator produces the buffer type, the serializer, and the send/receive systems. The buffer is a ring of the last ~64 ticks, not a single value, because the server needs history, and because rollback needs to replay it.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a circular D M A buffer with a timestamp per slot. The producer writes at the head; the consumer reads by timestamp, not by position.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Stages 2 and 5 are the ones nobody expects, and they are why the design works:

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Stage 5 is the magic. During a rollback replaying ticks 100, 110, this group re-materialises the exact input from tick 100, then 101, and so on. Your movement system reads Player Move Input and never knows it is in a replay.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Three details that are all load-bearing:

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: With All<Ghost Owner Is Local>(), without it you would write input into every player's capsule in your world. Net Code adds this tag to ghosts whose Ghost Owner.Network Id matches yours. No [Burst Compile], Keyboard.current is managed. Correct, not a compromise. Client Simulation only, the server must never invent input.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Our capsule uses Auto Command Target. Nerve also sets Command Target on the connection via Player Connection System, because Nerve supports controlling different pawns over time.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Trap, if input reaches the client's own capsule but the server never moves, suspect routing first. The client is happily predicting with input the server has no reason to associate with that entity.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Each command packet contains the last few ticks of input, not just one. Lose a packet and the next one still carries the missing tick. This is why unreliable transport is acceptable for input: the redundancy is in the payload, not the protocol.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Probe, Play Mode Tools shows command age and how many commands the server is holding. A steadily growing age means the client's prediction lead is drifting.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: This is the heart of the machine, and you have built it before, in silicon.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a branch predictor with speculative execution and a pipeline flush. The client speculates forward on predicted input. The server is the branch resolution unit. On a mispredict, you flush and replay from the checkpoint. Same structure, same costs, same failure modes.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Round trip is 50 milliseconds. If the client waited for the server to confirm every step, pressing W would move your capsule 50 milliseconds later. Unplayable.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: So the client does not wait. It applies your input immediately, assuming the server will agree. Usually it does.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Every step of that replay runs your systems, with the input from the command ring buffer for that exact tick. Which is why chapter 16's stage 5 exists.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Simulate: the one bit that makes it work

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Simulate is an enableable tag component. Before each tick of the prediction loop, Net Code enables it on exactly the ghosts that should simulate that tick and disables it on the rest.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: THE TRAP, omit With All<Simulate>() and your system integrates every predicted entity on every iteration of the rollback loop. Replaying 10 ticks moves the capsule 10× too far. It looks fine on a perfect connection and disintegrates the moment a packet drops. This is the single most common Net Code bug, and it only appears under exactly the conditions that are hardest to reproduce.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Think of Simulate as the clock-enable line on a register. The clock is running; the enable decides who latches this edge.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Why our movement system is written the way it is

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: There is no client version and no server version. One rule, executed twice. That is what "server-authoritative with client prediction" actually means in code.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Anything inside the prediction group can run many times for the same tick. Therefore:

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Every predicted ghost carries Predicted Ghost { Applied Tick, Prediction Start Tick }. It tells you which server tick the current state was last corrected from. Useful for debugging: if Applied Tick is far behind Server Tick, this ghost has not been corrected in a while.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Quantization. The server's float, quantized and dequantized, is not bit-identical. Input timing. A command arriving one tick late changes the server's simulation. Other players. You cannot predict what someone else pressed. Their capsule affects yours; your prediction of the shared world was wrong. Server-only events. A pickup despawning, a door opening.

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: Small rollbacks every few seconds are normal and healthy. Continuous large rollbacks mean your prediction is genuinely diverging, look at floating-point non-determinism, at uninitialised state, and at systems missing Simulate.

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: Rollback cost = (ticks to replay) × (cost of your predicted systems). A 200 milliseconds spike at 60 hertz is 12 replayed ticks in one frame. If your predicted simulation costs 2 milliseconds, that frame costs 24 milliseconds and you drop it.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, deeper pipeline, more expensive flush. Same engineering answer: keep the predicted set small, keep predicted systems cheap, and do not predict what does not need to feel instant.

chapters.title: b28
chapters.text: Probe, Play Mode Tools then prediction stats shows ticks-per-frame. Sustained values above 1 mean you are replaying constantly.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Prediction is for the entity you control. Interpolation is for everything else, and it is the cheaper, calmer half of the system.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Snapshots arrive every ~50 milliseconds (20 hertz send rate is common) while you render every ~7 milliseconds. You cannot show the newest snapshot the instant it arrives; you would get a slideshow with teleports.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: So the client renders in the past, between two snapshots it already has:

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Always between two known-good points. Never extrapolating. Never guessing.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Prediction vs interpolation, side by side

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: In our game both are on screen at once. Your capsule is drawn ~25 milliseconds ahead of the server; the other player's is drawn ~100 milliseconds behind. Neither of you sees "now". Nobody ever does.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, an elastic buffer between two clock domains. You accept latency to absorb jitter. Make it too small and you underrun (visible stutter); too large and you add pointless lag. Same knob, same trade, same tuning instinct.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Ghost Importance and the interpolation buffer

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: The buffer must hold enough history to bracket the interpolation tick even when packets drop. Net Code sizes it from the tick rate and observed jitter. If a ghost's data is missing for the bracketing ticks, the client holds the last known value, which reads as a brief freeze rather than a teleport. That is the correct failure mode.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: You can. Default Ghost Mode = Predicted on every ghost, and every client simulates the whole world. Fighting games and some shooters do this.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Every ghost replays on every rollback. Cost scales with predicted entities × replayed ticks. Every predicted entity must be deterministic across machines. Physics, if predicted, must be deterministic, which is a large commitment.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Owner Predicted says: pay that price for exactly the one entity where latency is unacceptable, and take the cheap smooth path for everything else. For a capsule game it is free correctness.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: When a rollback moves your predicted capsule, snapping is visible. Net Code can blend the visual position toward the corrected one over a few frames (Ghost Prediction Smoothing / Smoothing Action).

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Trap, smoothing operates on the rendered transform, not the simulated one. Never read a smoothed value back into simulation, or you have built a feedback loop between presentation and truth. Presentation reads from simulation. Never the reverse.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: What to check when the other capsule looks wrong

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Probe, Ghost Snapshot Inspector shows arrival timing per ghost. Irregular arrival with regular sends means the problem is the wire, not your code.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Part III done. You now know the wire. Time to trace one keypress all the way through it.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Eight steps from "socket" to "I can move my capsule". Learn this chain and you can diagnose any join failure in about ninety seconds.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Probe, this one command answers "where did it stop": ``csharp foreach (var w in World.All) { var em = w.Entity Manager; var conn = em.Create Entity Query(Component Type.Read Only<Network Stream Connection>()); var in Game = em.Create Entity Query(Component Type.Read Only<Network Stream Connection>(), Component Type.Read Only<Network Stream In Game>()); var ghosts = em.Create Entity Query(Component Type.Read Only<Ghost Instance>()); Debug.Log($"{w.Name}: conns={conn.Calculate Entity Count()} " + $"in Game={in Game.Calculate Entity Count()} ghosts={ghosts.Calculate Entity Count()}"); } ` conns=1 in Game=0 then step 5 or 6. in Game=1 ghosts=0` then step 7.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Both approval systems disable themselves when network.require-connection-approval is false, which is the default:

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: So on a stock project nothing ever adds Connection Approved, and Player Connection System requires it. No player ever spawns, and nothing is logged.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Turning approval on is not a free switch either: Connection Approval Server System only skips J W T validation when World.Is Server() is false, a purely local world. A separate Server World in one process is a server world, so it takes the real branch and calls Unity Authentication over the network.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Our Local Approve Connection System fills the gap with Account Identity = "local-{network Id}", labelled as a hack in its own doc comment, with the delete condition written down.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Network Stream In Game is the flag that arms the entire snapshot system. Nerve sends the request from a node, Bovine Labs.Nerve.State/States/Client/Go In Game.cs, that runs inside a client Grove graph. The sample ships a service graph and a menu graph. It ships no client graph. So the node existed and never executed.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Disconnect Reason tells you which: Timeout, Closed By Remote, Connection Close, Max Connection Attempts, Approval Failure, Protocol Error.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Nerve draws one more distinction worth stealing: a disconnect is voluntary only if it is Connection Close and you had already entered the game. Quitting looks different from being kicked at the door, and the UI should say different things.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Trap, connection events live for one tick. If you poll them from a system that does not run every tick, you will miss disconnects intermittently. Latch them into durable state the moment you see them, which is precisely what the tracker node does.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: The full trace. One W press, two capsules, two screens. Every hop, in order.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: This is the chapter the whole book exists for. If you can narrate this from memory, you are done.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Key contact closes. Keyboard controller debounces, sends a HID report over USB. Host controller raises an interrupt. Kernel HID driver decodes, queues an evdev event. Display server delivers it to the focused window. Unity's message pump drains it.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Input System updates Keyboard.current. This is managed memory. Player Gather Input System runs in Ghost Input System Group. Not bursted, it touches managed input. It filters With All<Ghost Owner Is Local>() so it writes only your capsule's Player Move Input. Player Move Input.Move = (1, 0) for W. Intent. Four bytes. Not a position.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Copy Input To Command Buffer System Group (Order Last) copies the component into Input Buffer Data<Player Move Input>[current Tick], a ring slot stamped with the tick. Command Send System serialises the last few ticks (built-in redundancy) and sends unreliably.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Copy Command Buffer To Input System Group (Order First inside Predicted Simulation System Group) reads the ring slot for the tick being simulated back into the component. Player Move System runs with With All<Simulate, Ghost Owner>(). Simulate is the clock-enable. Delta is one tick. Local Transform.Position += (1,0,0)·Speed·dt. Your capsule has already moved, zero frames after the keypress.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Packet crosses I P C or loopback U D P. Command Receive System writes into the server's own Input Buffer Data ring for that ghost.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: Server reaches that tick. Copy Command Buffer To Input System Group materialises the input. The same Player Move System, one [World System Filter] covering both worlds, runs. Same constant, same delta, same maths. Server's Local Transform is now the truth. If the client had lied, it would not matter: the server never received a position, only a direction.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Ghost Send System collects, prioritises, delta-compresses against each connection's ACKed baseline, and sends.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Ghost Receive System compares the received state for tick T with what you predicted for T. Match then nothing happens. Mismatch then restore and replay ticks T+1.now, re-feeding stored input each tick. You never see it.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Same snapshot arrives. Their copy of your capsule is interpolated, drawn between two received snapshots, roughly 100 milliseconds behind the server. Smooth, slightly stale, never wrong.

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Entities.Graphics uploads Local To World matrices to G P U buffers, issues batched draws. U R P renders. Present blocks on vsync. Photons.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: Both players see a different world, and both are correct. Server-authoritative multiplayer is the engineering discipline of making that disagreement invisible.

chapters.title: b29
chapters.text: Probe, the one-liner that separates the first three rows: ``csharp // in Client World and Server World, per tick Debug.Log($"{world.Name} move={input.Move} pos={transform.Position}"); ` If client move is non-zero and server move` is zero, it is hop 12, 14. Every time.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: A worked example of the whole stack: Grove + Canopy + Nerve + settings routing, doing one real job.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Something must add Network Stream In Game to the client's connection and send a Go In Game Request remote procedure call. Without it, zero snapshots flow (chapter 13).

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Nerve already ships the node that does this. It just never runs, because running it requires a client graph and the sample authors none.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: The chain state then Initialize then Startup Gate then Client Go In Game looks like ceremony. It is not, the types force it:

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: So: a state can run a block; only Initialize can drive a context node; only Startup Gate provides Initialize State; only inside it can Client Go In Game exist.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, this is type-level pin compatibility. You cannot plug a 3.3 V part into a 5 V header because the connector will not accept it. The graph editor enforces the same thing, at author time.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Every block AND-s into Is Completed. The gate jumps only when all report done. It is a barrier with a target, and it is reusable for any "wait for N things, then advance".

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: Idempotent by identity, not by boolean. Keying on the connection identity means a reconnect with a new entity re-sends correctly, while a retry on the same connection does not spam. State lives in Grove State, not in a static. Works per entity, survives, costs nothing. The gate is the retry loop. No timers, no coroutines.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Nerve ships the nodes. It does not ship a context or a driver, those are per-project, exactly like the sample's Menu and Service ones.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Trap, Get Execution returns a copy of the context. Assign before it and your values are overwritten by Update(); assign after and they land. Get this backwards and the graph runs with a zeroed connection forever, silently.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: A single world carrying both flags. Our separate Client World + Server World in one process is not a host, Is Host() is false for both. That is correct here: it makes Go In Game add Network Stream In Game on the client side, which is exactly what a real client needs.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Assets/Editor/Client Graph Setup.cs, [Menu Item("Daggertooth/Rebuild Client Graph")]. Same approach as Nerve's own Sample Project Setup. Advantages over clicking in the graph window:

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: reviewable in a diff reproducible in CI validation failures throw instead of logging the helper prints every available option name when Try Set Value fails

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Delete the old workaround system, run, and ask the graph where it is:

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: in Game=1 proves the remote procedure call went out. state = gameplay proves the graph sent it, that state is reachable only through the gate, and the gate opens only when the node reports completed. No leftover code can produce that reading.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: That is what a falsifiable check looks like: a value that is impossible unless the mechanism you claim is working, worked.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Who is allowed to move what, and how does a capsule exist in the first place.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Ghost Owner Is Local is the one you filter input on (chapter 16). Ghost Owner is the one you filter rules on, our Player Move System uses With All<Simulate, Ghost Owner>() so it moves player-owned things on both client and server.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Nerve does not spawn one thing. It spawns two, and the split is worth copying:

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Why bother? Because "the player" and "the thing the player is currently driving" are different lifetimes:

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Respawn then new pawn, same controller, score and identity intact. Enter a vehicle then controller re-points at the vehicle; input follows. Spectate then controller with no pawn. Reconnect then match by Account Identity, re-attach to the existing controller.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, the controller is a stable device handle; the pawn is the currently mapped buffer. You re-point the handle; you do not tear down the session.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: This is why our two-player run shows 4 ghosts: 2 controllers + 2 capsules. Seeing 3 would mean two connections adopted the same controller, an identity collision, which is exactly the risk Account Identity = "local-{network Id}" carries and which the 4-ghost reading disproves.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Every one of those must be present. Chapter 19's ladder is really just "which of these four is missing".

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Looks for an existing controller with the same Account Identity (reconnect path). If none, instantiates Server Settings.player Controller. Instantiates Server Settings.player Character as the controlled entity. Links them (Primary Controlled Entity), sets Ghost Owner.Network Id on both. Points the connection's Command Target at the pawn.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Controller Ownership Initialize System then propagates ownership down linked entity groups, so a pawn with child entities has them all owned consistently.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Miss any link and the failure is silent. The most common misses, in order of frequency:

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: The Object Definition is not in Object Management Settings then ID resolves to nothing. The settings asset is not on the Settings Authoring prefab then never bakes. The prefab is missing Ghost Authoring Component then spawns, but only on the server. Has Owner unchecked then no Ghost Owner then input filters match nothing.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Trap, we hit a fifth: Player Move Input Authoring was declared inside Player Move Input.cs. Unity only creates a Mono Script when the file name matches the class name, so the component serialised as m_Script: {file ID: 0}, a missing script. It baked nothing, the capsule spawned with no input component, and nothing anywhere complained. One Mono Behaviour per file, named after the file. Always.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: The client writes exactly one thing: what it wants. Everything else it receives. That single sentence is the security model.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Probe, who owns what, right now: ``csharp foreach (var (owner, e) in System API.Query<Ref RO<Ghost Owner>>().With Entity Access()) Debug.Log($"{e} owned by Network Id {owner.Value RO.Network Id}"); ``

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Multiplayer Play Mode (multiplayer play mode) runs extra editor instances, virtual players, that share your project folder and attach to the same play session. It is how you test two clients without building.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: A virtual player is a real second editor process with its own World.All, its own sockets, and its own domain. It shares your Editor Prefs, and Client Server Bootstrap.Requested Play Type is stored there.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: The console error is a port-bind exception followed by a cascade, Mod Loading Scene found 2 instances, entity assertion failures. The cascade is louder than the cause, which is why it misleads.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: The obvious fix, "change Play Mode Type to Client in Play Mode Tools", does not work, because Play Mode Tools is a window in the main editor and a virtual player does not have one. The pref you would change is the shared one you must not change.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Installing com.unity.dedicated-server defines UNITY_USE_MULTIPLAYER_ROLES as a version Define. That flips Multiplayer Play Mode Preferences from the shared-Editor Prefs path to the per-player-role path, and each virtual player gets its own dropdown.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: A visible confirmation that the switch took effect: Play Mode Type in Play Mode Tools goes grey. Roles now override it, so the old control is disabled. If it is still editable, the define is not active.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, you were trying to configure two boards by editing one shared EEPROM. Roles give each board its own strapping pins.

chapters.title: b16

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: The most you-shaped chapter in the book. No E C S, no networking, just the dynamic linker, sonames, and a search-path rule that is not transitive.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Unity 6000.7.0a3 on Ubuntu 26.04. The editor exits with code 127, or launches fine and then every multiplayer play mode virtual player dies with:

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: A soname bump (.so.2 then.so.16) is an ABI break declaration. That is the whole point of sonames. So ln -s libxml2.so.16 libxml2.so.2 is not a fix, it is a promise you cannot keep, and it will pay out months later somewhere unrelated.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: The machine had a stale ldconfig cache entry pointing at libxml2.so.2 inside an uninstalled older editor. The file was gone; the cache still advertised it. Some paths worked by accident.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Running sudo ldconfig cleared the stale entry, and turned "working by accident" into a clean, honest exit 127.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Trap, I called ldconfig "free". It was not. It was load-bearing garbage. A cache rebuild is only free if the cache is describing reality, and a stale entry pointing at a deleted file is precisely the case where it is not. The general rule: never run a "harmless refresh" on state you have not inspected. The refresh is harmless; discovering what the state was actually doing is not.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: The fix, and why the obvious version fails

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Step one: put the right library, with the right soname, next to the editor.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: And it still fails. Here is why, and it is the good part:

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: THE MECHANISM, run path is not transitive. Unity's binary has a run path containing $ORIGIN, so the loader finds Editor/libxml2.so.2. But when the loader then resolves libxml2's own DT_NEEDED entry for libicui18n.so.74, it does not consult Unity's run path. run path applies only to the direct dependencies of the object that declares it. (RPATH, the deprecated predecessor, was transitive. run path deliberately is not, that was the point of introducing it.)

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: L D library path, by contrast, is consulted for every object in the process. So:

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: The wrapper also fixes multiplayer play mode, because virtual players are child processes and inherit the environment. One export, every process.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Note L D library path outranks run path. That ordering is exactly what makes the wrapper work.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Because a soname is a contract. Two generations of the same library in the global namespace will resolve fine for months and then break something unrelated, at the worst time, with no trail. Scoping to Editor/ means only Unity sees the old ABI, which is precisely what 6000.7.0a2 was doing before the regression.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Trap, an editor upgrade replaces Unity and silently removes the wrapper. Re-apply after every upgrade, or script it.

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: A soname bump is an ABI break. Never alias across one. run path is not transitive; L D library path is. This single fact explains a huge class of "I copied the.so and it still can't find it" bugs. Scope compatibility shims as narrowly as possible. Process-local beats system-wide, always. A stale cache entry can be load-bearing. Inspect before you refresh. ldd is your nm here. When a process will not start, ask the loader, not the app.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: The final exam. Not "can you use this stack", could you write it?

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: Below is what each layer would cost you, what the hard part actually is, and the order to attempt it in. Build even two of these and you will never be confused by the real ones again.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: The hard part is not the layout. It is the structural change: adding a component means computing the new archetype, finding or creating a chunk, memcpy-ing every component, patching the entity lookup, and invalidating outstanding pointers. Get that right and the rest is bookkeeping.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Milestone: 100k entities, one component write each, faster than the array-of-structs version.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: You are writing a linker and an interpreter.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: The hard part is relative addressing. Every pointer inside the image must be an offset from its own location, so the whole thing is memcpy-able and shareable. That is Blob Ptr<T>, and it is the same discipline as writing position-independent code.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Milestone: author a 5-node graph, save it, load it into a fresh process, execute it with zero allocations.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Layer 3 · A hierarchical state machine, two days

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: states form a tree; the active path is root then leaf Enter / Update / Exit signals propagate along the path transitions are named jumps, resolved by hash validate at author time: one root, one default child per composite, no id collisions

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: The hard part is exit/enter ordering. Exit bottom-up, enter top-down, and never let a block observe a half-torn-down path. That is why every Canopy node opens with the Exit check.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Milestone: a graph where a leaf jump correctly exits three levels and enters two.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Layer 4 · Snapshot replication, two weeks

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: The hard part is per-connection baselines. Every client has ACKed a different tick, so the server must remember what each one knows and delta against that. Get it wrong and clients decode garbage, intermittently, under loss only.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Milestone: 50 entities, 20 hertz, 5% simulated packet loss, no visible corruption.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Layer 5 · Prediction and rollback, the real boss

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: The hard part is that your simulation must be replayable. Which means:

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: no reads of frame-varying data (frame delta, Time.time, Random without a seeded state) no side effects that are not idempotent per tick all predicted state must be in the checkpoint, anything stored outside it silently survives the rollback and desyncs

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: That last bullet is the one that bites. A cached value in a system field is invisible to the checkpoint and will corrupt every replay.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Milestone: 200 milliseconds artificial latency, capsule feels instant, no visible correction.

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: If you can describe all five, you can read any networked engine, Unreal's replication, Photon Quantum, Overwatch's E C S talk, Rocket League's rollback. They are the same five layers with different names and different trade-offs.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: A chunk is a D M A buffer and an archetype is its type. A blob is position-independent code; Grove State is its RAM. Simulate is a clock-enable line. Send intent, never results. Nobody on screen is seeing "now", and your job is to make that invisible.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Grove has more than "nodes". It has kinds, and the kind decides what the blob holds and how dispatch reaches it.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Two dispatch verbs, not one: Execute (side effects, returns nothing) and Calculate (pure, returns T). That split is why data ports can be evaluated lazily and why a data node can be shared by several execution nodes without ordering problems.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Three rules that fall out of this layout:

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Blob Ptr<T> is a relative offset. The image is position-independent, so it can be memcpy'd, cached, and shared read-only by every entity. The image is immutable at runtime. No node may write to it. All mutable state goes in Grove State. Graph Id disambiguates. Two entities running different graphs keep separate state because the key includes the graph id.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, you are looking at a flashed image with a header table. Root is the reset vector. Nodes[] is the code segment. Inputs/Outputs is the symbol table.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Keys are built by Graph State Util.Get Key(.) from three ingredients:

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Values are blittable structs stored inline. No allocation, Burst-safe, per entity, and it survives across ticks and across rollbacks (it lives on the entity, so it is checkpointed with everything else).

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Trap, do not cache node state in a static or in a system field. It will not be per entity, it will not be checkpointed, and under prediction rollback it will silently desync. Grove State exists precisely to make the right thing easy.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: That last row is the performance secret and the compile-time cost. Every context type gets its own monomorphised dispatch, no generic virtual calls, everything inlinable, Burst sees concrete types all the way down.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Forget partial and you get a wall of "does not implement IContext Generator<T>" errors that point at the interface rather than at the missing keyword.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Containers: how a node reaches component data

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Set Chunk(chunk, index) refreshes them once per chunk; nodes then index by grove Context.Entity Index In Chunk. That is why per-entity access inside a node is an array index, not a lookup, the expensive part happened once per chunk.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: Two ways to reuse one graph with different numbers:

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Both are resolved at bake time, so the runtime image is already specialised. There is no runtime branch and no lookup cost. It is template instantiation, done by the baker.

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Graph Options.Supports Subgraphs is on for all three Nerve graph types. A subgraph is a whole.cnerve/.snerve referenced as one node, with its own scope in Grove Node State (see Push Subgraph Scope). Scoping means node ids inside a subgraph do not collide with the parent, so the same subgraph can appear twice in one graph with independent state.

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a subgraph is a linked library with its own symbol namespace, instantiated at link time rather than called at runtime.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: Disable Auto Inclusion Of Nodes From Graph Assembly

chapters.title: b28
chapters.text: Without this flag, Graph Toolkit would offer every node in the assembly in every graph. With it, a node appears only where [Use With Graph(.)] says. That is why a.snerve cannot contain Client Go In Game Node, and why adding a node to the wrong graph type is impossible rather than merely wrong.

chapters.title: b30
chapters.text: UNITY_INCLUDE_INSTRUMENTATION compiles a debug pass that walks every node after execution and calls Debug(.) on it, plus a Selected Entity singleton so the graph window can show live values for one entity. It is off in players and costs nothing there.

chapters.title: b32
chapters.text: The hash lookups are the only non-trivial per-entity cost. If a graph is hot, the first optimisation is fewer keyed state values, not fewer nodes.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: A reference chapter. Each setting: what it does, what it costs, and how to choose.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: 1 · Tick and send rate, Client Server Tick Rate

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: The one people miss: Network Tick Rate is separate from Simulation Tick Rate. Simulating at 60 and sending at 20 is the standard shape, three sims per snapshot, one third of the bandwidth, and interpolation hides the difference.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: Batching kicks in when the server falls behind: it merges several ticks into one step with a larger delta. It protects against a death spiral and it degrades input fidelity. If you see the batching warning outside of editor hitches, your server tick is genuinely too expensive.

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Optimization Mode.Static is the cheapest win in the whole system. A static ghost that has not changed is not serialised, not delta-compared, and not sent. For level props and parked vehicles it removes them from the bandwidth budget entirely.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: 3 · Per-field replication, [Ghost Field]

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: [Ghost Component(.)] controls the component as a whole:

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Design rule, Owner Send Type = Send To Owner on anything only the owner needs (ammo, cooldowns, private state) is both a bandwidth saving and an anti-cheat measure: information you never send cannot be extracted.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: Quantization error is 0.5 / Quantization in world units.

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Too coarse and the client's prediction disagrees with the dequantized server value every tick, producing constant micro-rollbacks that read as jitter. Too fine and you pay bits for precision no one can see. Match it to your world scale, not to a habit.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Importance vs relevancy is the distinction to internalise:

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Use relevancy for zones, rooms, and fog of war. Use importance for everything that is visible but not equally urgent. Relevancy is also a security boundary: a client cannot wall-hack data it was never sent.

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Prediction switching is the advanced move: predict only the ghosts near the local player, interpolate the rest, and reassign as they approach. It keeps rollback cost bounded in a crowded world. Budget it by predicted entity count, because rollback cost is predicted entities × replayed ticks.

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: Runs after a rollback and blends the rendered value toward the corrected one.

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Trap, smoothing must never feed back into simulation. Presentation reads simulation; the reverse is a feedback loop that diverges.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Always develop with emulation on. 80 milliseconds round trip time and 2% loss as your daily setting will surface every prediction bug while it is still cheap. A LAN-perfect connection hides exactly the class of bug that ships.

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: Nerve wraps this in a Relevancy Settings asset, which our project registers on Server Settings.prefab.

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: Thin clients are the cheapest scale test you will ever write: no rendering, no presentation, real connections, real commands. Give them a fake-input system and you can put 50 players on your laptop.

lessons.title: 30 · How it is made to feel nice

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Every trick in this chapter exists to hide the same fact: information takes time to travel, and players will not forgive it. These are the mechanisms, ranked by how much perceived quality they buy.

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: A 60 milliseconds round trip time with no prediction puts you at "sluggish" on every single input. That is the problem the entire stack is arranged around.

chapters.title: b5
chapters.text: 1 · Prediction, buys the most, costs the most

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Perceived input latency: zero. The price is a replay whenever the server disagrees, and a hard requirement that your simulation is replayable (chapter 17).

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: 2 · Interpolation, buys smoothness for everyone else

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Rendering other players in the past, between two known snapshots, converts irregular arrival into regular motion. It is a jitter buffer, and it is why a 20 hertz snapshot rate can look like 144 hertz motion.

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: 3 · Partial ticks, buys smoothness between ticks

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Simulate at 60, render at 144, and 60% of frames have nothing new. Partial ticks run a fraction of a tick purely for presentation, then throw it away.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Trap, one-shot effects must be gated on Is First Time Fully Predicting Tick, or they fire on every partial tick too.

chapters.title: b12
chapters.text: 4 · Command redundancy, buys resilience to loss for free

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Each command packet contains the last several ticks of input, not just one. A dropped packet costs nothing because the next one carries the gap. This is why input feels solid on a lossy connection while positions still visibly hitch.

chapters.title: b14
chapters.text: 5 · Snapshot delta compression, buys bandwidth, which buys rate

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Only changed fields are sent, delta-coded against what each client last ACKed. Fewer bits per ghost means more ghosts per packet means a higher effective update rate for everything.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: Quantization amplifies this: quantized values compare equal more often, so more fields are "unchanged".

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: 6 · Importance scheduling, buys the illusion of a full world

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: The server cannot send everything. It sends the most important things this tick and defers the rest. Nearby, moving, dangerous things update at a high rate; distant scenery updates occasionally. The player perceives a fully live world because the parts they are looking at are live.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: 7 · Correction smoothing, buys invisibility for the fix

chapters.title: b20
chapters.text: When a rollback moves your capsule, snapping is visible. Blending the rendered position over a few frames hides small corrections entirely. Above Max Smoothing Distance it snaps instead, because sliding a long way looks worse than a clean cut.

chapters.title: b22
chapters.text: The advanced one. The client shoots at what it sees, which is the past. Naively, the server checks against the present and the shot misses.

chapters.title: b23
chapters.text: Track Interpolation Delay on the ghost is what makes the server able to reconstruct "what did this client see". The trade is real and famous: behind cover and still shot. Every shooter picks a point on that spectrum; none escape it.

chapters.title: b24
chapters.text: 9 · Time synchronisation, buys stability under changing conditions

chapters.title: b25
chapters.text: The client continuously measures round trip time and jitter, then adjusts:

chapters.title: b26
chapters.text: how far ahead it predicts (so commands land just in time) how far behind it interpolates (so the buffer never underruns)

chapters.title: b27
chapters.text: It does this by nudging the rate of local time, not by jumping. Slow drift is invisible; a jump is not.

chapters.title: b28
chapters.text: Hardware analogy, a PLL. You do not step the clock; you adjust its frequency and let phase converge. Same reason: discontinuities are what people notice.

chapters.title: b30
chapters.text: Ghosts marked Optimization Mode.Static that have not changed are skipped entirely. Every ghost you can mark static is bandwidth handed back to the ghosts that need it.

chapters.title: b32
chapters.text: Six independent mechanisms, each hiding one consequence of the same physical fact. None of them removes latency. They relocate it to places players do not look.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: Decision tables. Keep this chapter open while designing a feature.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: A · How should this data reach the other side?

chapters.title: b4
chapters.text: Rule, if you are about to send an remote procedure call every tick, you wanted a ghost field. If you are about to put a one-shot event in a ghost field, you wanted an remote procedure call.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: Cost check: rollback cost is predicted entities × replayed ticks. Every entity you add to the predicted set multiplies every correction.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Pre-spawned is free and badly under-used. If it exists at level load and the server does not create it, bake it.

chapters.title: b10
chapters.text: Raise sim rate for simulation fidelity. Raise send rate for visual freshness. They are different problems.

chapters.title: b15
chapters.text: Our project uses both, correctly: Player Move System is a plain system (one rule, no states); the connection flow is a graph (states, gates, transitions, recovery).

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: J · Quick sanity table for a new feature

chapters.title: b18
chapters.text: Before writing a line, answer these six:

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Question 6 is the one people skip. For our client graph the answer was state = gameplay, a value unreachable unless the mechanism worked.

chapters.title: b2
chapters.text: One feature, designed end to end, touching every layer. Follow this and the stack stops being a list of packages and becomes one machine.

chapters.title: b3
chapters.text: The feature: a dash. Tap Shift, the capsule lunges forward, then a cooldown before you can dash again. It must feel instant, be cheat-proof, and be visible to the other player.

chapters.title: b6
chapters.text: IInput Component Data supports event-style fields that survive the tick they were pressed on:

chapters.title: b7
chapters.text: Input Event exists precisely because a bool sampled per frame and consumed per tick loses presses. It carries a counter so the consumer can tell "pressed once" from "still held" even across a rollback.

chapters.title: b8
chapters.text: Step 3 · Replicated state for the cooldown

chapters.title: b9
chapters.text: A tick, not a float timer. Ticks are the shared clock; a float seconds value would drift between the two simulations and desync under replay.

chapters.title: b11
chapters.text: Every constraint from the book is visible here:

chapters.title: b13
chapters.text: Without that gate the effect fires on every partial tick and on every replayed tick of every rollback. This is the single most common "why does my gun fire three times" bug.

chapters.title: b16
chapters.text: If dashing should be blocked in a menu, or should trigger a state change, add a Grove node. If it is just a rule, leave it as a system. Chapter 31, table H.

chapters.title: b17
chapters.text: For a dash: leave it a system. No states, no transitions, no designer-facing flow.

chapters.title: b19
chapters.text: Step 6 is the important one. A check that cannot fail is not a check. Break the thing on purpose once, confirm your test catches it, then fix it. That is the difference between "I believe it works" and "I know what would tell me it didn't".

chapters.title: b21
chapters.text: Six steps. Every multiplayer feature you will ever build fits them. Weapons, vehicles, abilities, inventory, doors, the answers change, the questions do not.
